<meta>continues from previous page: and the nature</meta>of paths and circles so positioned that they affect those looking at them at a certain time. Thus ships, although they go with full sails, nevertheless seem to stand still. There will be someone who demonstrates at some time in which parts of the heavens the comets wander, why they travel so separated from the rest, and how large and of what kind they are. We are content with what has been discovered; let posterity also contribute something to the truth. Through the stars, he says, we do not see things beyond, but through comets we transmit our sight. First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself consists of thick and solid fire, but where a thin splendor runs out and disperses into hair <note>original: "crines", referring to the comet's tail</note>. You see through the gaps between the fires, not through the fires themselves. All stars, he says, are round; comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars. Who indeed will grant you that comets are long, when their nature is indeed a globe like the rest? However, their brightness is extended just as the sun sends out its rays far and wide. Yet the form of the body itself is one thing, and the light that flows from it is another. Thus the body of comets itself is rounded, but their splendor appears longer than that of other stars. 

"Why?" you ask. Tell me first, why does the moon receive a light so unlike the sun's, even though it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a leaden and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have faces somewhat unlike one another, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars even if they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the others, even if they do not have a similar face to them. Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in <term>Leo</term> <gloss>the Lion</gloss> and parches the lands with heat, while in <term>Aquarius</term> <gloss>the Water-bearer</gloss> it tightens the winter and closes the rivers with frost? Yet both this and that constellation are of the same condition <margin>† rises</margin> <note>The symbol indicates a textual variant or correction in the original manuscript</note>, though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time <term>Aries</term> <gloss>the Ram</gloss> † rises, while <term>Libra</term> <gloss>the Scales</gloss> sinks most slowly; and yet this constellation and that are of the same nature, although the former ascends in a brief time and the latter is drawn out for a long time. 

Do you not see how contrary the elements are to one another? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The whole harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, is that star <note>Saturn</note> which returns to its place in the thirtieth year very similar to this one <note>the sun or moon</note> which revisits its seat within a year? Nature does not present her work according to a single form, but prides herself on variety. She made some things slower, others faster than the rest. Some stronger, others more temperate; some she led out from the crowd so that they might proceed individually and conspicuously, and some she sent into a flock. He is ignorant of nature's power who does not think she is permitted to do at any time except what she does often. 

She does not show comets frequently; she assigned them another place, other times, and motions unlike the rest. She wished to celebrate the magnitude of her work through these, whose appearance is more beautiful than what you might think accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the others. Indeed, their appearance has something remarkable and singular, not thrown together and narrowed into a small space, but released more freely, embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a star which announces future events? For this is not a sign of a storm in the same way that sparking oil or the growth of rot-fungi <note>snuff forming on a lamp wick</note> are signs of future rain, or in the same way that it is an indication of a raging sea if sea-coots play on dry land and desert their familiar marshes, and the heron flies above the high cloud. But rather like the equinox of the year turning toward heat and cold. 

Just as those things which the <term>Chaldeans</term> <gloss>astrologers</gloss> sing, regarding what a star determines as sad or joyful for those being born. So that you may know this is so, a comet's rising does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspicious.</margin> it makes the whole year suspicious. From which it appears that it did not draw signs from things close at hand to give to things close at hand, but has them stored up and compressed by the laws of the world. This was done by the comet that appeared in the consulship of Patruculus and Vopiscus <note>approximately 15 AD</note>, which things were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were great and continuous storms everywhere. But in <term>Achaia</term> and <term>Macedonia</term>, cities were overthrown by earthquakes. 

"Their slowness," he says, "is proof that they are heavier and have much of the earthy in them. Furthermore, their very courses, for they are almost driven toward the poles." Both are false. I will speak of the first point first: that those things which are carried more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which completes its journey most slowly of all, heavy? And yet it has proof of lightness, because it is above the others. "But," you say, "it travels in a larger circuit,"

<summary>Seneca defends the celestial nature of comets by highlighting the diversity of the universe and arguing that rarity and unusual form do not disqualify them from being eternal stars. He disputes the idea that their slow motion indicates a heavy or earthy composition, using Saturn as a counter-example.</summary>

<keywords>comets, celestial mechanics, Aristotle, Saturn, planetary motion, astrology, weather signs, nature of the universe</keywords>
